Euphrates
ū-frā'tēz
n. (the great river of Mesopotamia — the fourth river of Eden, the northern bound of the promise, and the boundary of judgment in the Revelation)
From Hebrew Perath, probably from a root meaning to break forth or be fruitful; the Greek Euphrates comes through Old Persian Ufratu. In Hebrew it is often simply han-nahar, “the river”, as though no other needed naming.

Biblical Definition

The Euphrates is the Bible's great river, and it frames the whole story. It is the last of the four rivers of Eden — “And the fourth river is Euphrates” (Gen 2:14) — named without explanation because the first readers knew it. It is the northern limit of the land covenanted to Abram: “from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates” (Gen 15:18), a boundary reached only under David and Solomon. Beyond it lay Assyria and Babylon, so that crossing the river came to mean exile, and Jeremiah was sent to bury a girdle by it and later to sink a book in it as a sign of Babylon's sinking. Then in the Revelation it returns twice, at the sixth trumpet and the sixth vial: four angels “bound in the great river Euphrates” (Rev 9:14) loosed to slay; and the water “dried up, that the way of the kings of the east might be prepared” (Rev 16:12) — the same drying of a river that God had done at the Red Sea and Jordan, now done to open a road for judgment rather than for a redeemed people. From the garden to the last plagues, the same water: a boundary given, a boundary crossed in exile, and a boundary removed at the end.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) treats Euphrates in geography as the great river of Asia rising in Armenia and falling into the Persian gulf, the eastern boundary of the promised land.

expand to see more

EUPHRATES, n. A celebrated river of Asia, rising in the mountains of Armenia and running into the Persian gulf.

It is one of the four rivers named in the second chapter of Genesis as parting from the garden.

In Scripture it is emphatically called the great river, or simply the river.

It was assigned as the utmost bound of the land promised to the seed of Abraham.

Babylon stood upon it, and its waters were turned aside by Cyrus at the taking of the city.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:14 — "And the name of the third river is Hiddekel: that is it which goeth toward the east of Assyria. And the fourth river is Euphrates."

Gen 15:18 — "In the same day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates:"

Rev 9:14 — "Saying to the sixth angel which had the trumpet, Loose the four angels which are bound in the great river Euphrates."

Rev 16:12 — "And the sixth angel poured out his vial upon the great river Euphrates; and the water thereof was dried up, that the way of the kings of the east might be prepared."

Modern Corruption

Gen 2 is read as myth borrowed from Mesopotamia; the naming of two rivers still on every map is a strange feature for a myth, and the text plainly means a real place.

expand to see more

The four rivers of Eden are the standard exhibit for treating Gen 2 as borrowed Near Eastern mythology. It is worth noticing what the text actually does. Two of the four are named without gloss because everyone knew them — Hiddekel, which is the Tigris, and Euphrates — and two are located by the lands they compass. A myth does not usually anchor itself to rivers the reader can walk to. The account presents itself as geography attached to history, and the flood makes the surviving watercourses a testimony rather than a map of the antediluvian world. The dictionary holds a historical Adam in a real garden, and reads Gen 2:14 as the writer intended it.

The second matter is prophetic and calls for restraint. The Euphrates in Rev 9 and 16 has been fitted to every contemporary alignment of powers in the Middle East for two centuries, with a uniform record of failure. What the text asserts is plain enough without the newspaper: the barrier God set is removed at His word, a road is opened for the gathering to Armageddon, and the sequence is His. The dictionary does not hold dispensational premillennialism — a nineteenth-century novelty absent from every Reformation confession — and does not read the drying of the river as a datable geopolitical event. Read it as the sixth vial: the last restraints coming off before the end.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Perath (H6578), Euphrates; nahar (H5104), a river; Greek Euphrates (G2166).

expand to see more

Hebrew Perath (H6578) — Euphrates; from a root suggesting to break forth, to be fruitful.

Hebrew han-nahar hag-gadol — “the great river”; the standing epithet of Gen 15:18 and Deu 1:7.

Hebrew Chiddeqel (H2313) — Hiddekel, the Tigris; the third river of Eden, named with it.

Greek Euphrates (G2166) — Euphrates; used only in the Revelation, at the sixth trumpet and sixth vial.

Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to dry up; what God does to rivers to make a way, at the Red sea, at Jordan, and at the end.

Usage

"“And the fourth river is Euphrates” — a river of Eden still on the map."

"“Unto the great river, the river Euphrates” — the northern bound of the promise."

"“The water thereof was dried up” — the last barrier removed."
